why.support: Forms have rules. They tell you how to answer and where to go next. Learn the rules. Then you can fill in any form, right the first time.
why.core: Forms are texts with their own rules. They tell you **how** to answer (black pen, block letters, one box only) and **where** to go next. Once you can read those rules, forms stop being scary. Filling them in accurately, and spelling your details right, is how you get your Medicare card, your tax file number and your pay without delays.
why.extend: Forms are highly structured texts: their layout, instructions and navigation words control how you respond. Reading them closely, using precise form vocabulary and checking your answers before you sign means your applications go through first time, and your personal information stays safe.

articles.title: How to fill in a form

body.support:
Around 15, you'll fill in forms for a **tax file number** (TFN), a **bank account** and your own **Medicare card**. They all follow the same rules.

**1. Read the rules first.** *Black pen. BLOCK LETTERS. One box only.*

**2. Follow the arrows.** *If no, go to Question 9.* Skip what doesn't apply. Leave **Office use only** blank.

**3. Know the words.**

- **Family name** = last name. **Given names** = first and middle names.
- **Date of birth**: DD/MM/YYYY, like 07/03/2010.
- **Residential address** = where you live. **Postal address** = where your mail goes.

**4. Spell it right.** Check your name and address.

**5. Check, then sign.** The **declaration** says it's all true.

Give your TFN to your boss. If you don't, almost half your pay goes in tax!

Real government websites end in **.gov.au**.
body.core:
Around 15, the forms start: a **tax file number** (TFN) for your first job, a **bank account** for your pay, your own **Medicare card**. Forms can look scary, but they all follow the same rules.

**1. Read the instructions first.** Most forms start with rules: *Use a black pen. Print in BLOCK LETTERS. Mark one box only.* Online forms mark the questions you must answer with a star (*).

**2. Follow the navigation.** Forms are split into **sections** and numbered **questions**. Some questions send you somewhere else: *If no, go to Question 9.* Skip the questions that don't apply to you. Leave anything marked **Office use only** blank.

**3. Know the form words.**

- **Family name** is your last name. **Given names** are your first and middle names.
- **Date of birth** is often written DD/MM/YYYY, like 07/03/2010.
- Your **residential address** is where you actually live. Your **postal address** is where your mail goes.

**4. Spell it right.** Your name, address and school must match your other documents exactly. Check tricky words like *February* and *address*.

**5. Check before you sign.** The **declaration** says everything you wrote is true. Re-read every answer, fix mistakes neatly, and then sign and date it.

**Three forms you'll meet soon:**

- **TFN.** It's free from the ATO. Give it to your employer, or they must take out tax at the top rate: almost half your pay.
- **Medicare.** At 15, you can get your own Medicare card through myGov or a form.
- **Bank account.** You'll need to prove who you are, often with ID documents.

Finally, make sure the form is **real**. Government websites end in **.gov.au**, and applying for a TFN never costs money.
body.extend:
From about 15, official forms become part of life: a **tax file number** (TFN) for employment, a **bank account** for wages, and your own **Medicare card**. Each is a structured text whose conventions govern how you respond.

**1. Read the instructions.** Forms open with response rules: *black pen, BLOCK LETTERS, mark one box*. Online forms flag mandatory fields, often with an asterisk.

**2. Use the navigation.** Sections and numbered questions organise the form. Conditional instructions (*If no, go to Question 9*) route you past questions that don't apply. Never complete **Office use only** sections.

**3. Use form vocabulary precisely.**

- **Family name** (surname) and **given names** (first and middle).
- **Date of birth** in the requested format, often DD/MM/YYYY.
- **Residential** (where you live) versus **postal** address (where mail is delivered).

**4. Spell accurately.** Details must match your other identity documents exactly.

**5. Verify before you sign.** The **declaration** is a legal statement that your information is true and correct. Re-read, correct neatly, then sign and date.

**Three forms you'll meet soon:**

- **TFN.** Free from the ATO. Without it, employers must withhold tax at the top rate (47%).
- **Medicare.** From 15, you can get your own card via myGov or form MS011.
- **Bank account.** Banks must verify your identity.

Finally, verify the form itself. Government sites end in **.gov.au**, and the ATO never charges to apply for a TFN.

caseStudies.title: The sign-in page that wasn't real

body.support:
**myGov** is a government website. You sign in by typing your details.

In **2024**, the government warned about **fake myGov websites**. Scammers sent texts with links to fake sign-in pages. People typed in their details. The scammers stole them.

In one year, there were **more than 6,000** scams pretending to be myGov.

The advice:

- myGov will **never** text you a link to sign in.
- Type **my.gov.au** yourself.
- Real government sites end in **.gov.au**.

Only fill in a form if it's real.
body.core:
**myGov** is the government website where you can see your Medicare, tax and Centrelink details. Signing in means typing your details into a form.

In **April 2024**, the government warned Australians about **fake myGov websites**. Scammers sent emails and texts with links to pages that looked exactly like the real myGov sign-in form. When people typed in their details, the scammers captured them. They could then use those details to commit tax and refund fraud in someone else's name.

The government said Services Australia and its partners had responded to **more than 6,000 scams** pretending to be myGov in the previous year.

Its advice was simple:

- The ATO and myGov will **never** send you an email or text with a link to sign in.
- Type **my.gov.au** yourself, or use the myGov app.
- Real government websites end in **.gov.au**.

A form is only safe to fill in if it's **real**. Checking where it came from is part of reading it.
body.extend:
**myGov** is the government portal for Medicare, tax and Centrelink services. Signing in means entering personal details into an online form.

In **April 2024**, the federal government warned of a high volume of reports about **fake myGov websites**. Scam emails and texts linked to convincing copies of the myGov sign-in page. Details entered there were captured and could be used for tax and refund fraud in the victims' names.

The government reported that Services Australia and its partners had responded to **more than 6,000 scams** impersonating myGov in the previous year.

Its guidance:

- The ATO and myGov will **never** send an email or text containing a sign-in link.
- Navigate to **my.gov.au** directly, or use the myGov app.
- Official government websites end in **.gov.au**.

Evaluating a form's source is as important as completing it accurately. The safest form is one you reached yourself.

teacher.overview: Students learn to read forms as structured texts: instructions (black pen, block letters, mark one box), navigation (sections, numbered questions, conditional *go to* instructions, office use only), and form vocabulary (family and given names, date formats, residential and postal addresses, declaration, applicant, proof of identity). They practise accurate spelling of common form words, check answers against instructions, and learn to verify that an online form is genuine, using the government's 2024 warning about fake myGov sign-in pages.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** residential = where you live; postal = where your mail goes. Re-read because the declaration says it's all true and correct.

**Form:** 1 instructions; 2 family and given names; 3 date format DD/MM/YYYY; 4 residential address (not a PO box); 5 navigation (No → go to Q8); 6 declaration; 7 office use only (leave blank).

**Sort:** jordan — fix (block letters; a given name in the family name box); 21/11/2009 — looks right; PO box as residential — fix; same as residential — looks right; N/A in office use — fix (leave blank); 2009/11/21 — fix (wrong order).

**Spelling:** address (double d, double s), signature (sign + ature), separate (there's *a rat* in sep-a-rate), Wednesday (Wed-nes-day), occurred (double c, double r), receive (*i before e except after c*).

**Form words (samples):** family name — surname; applicant — the person asking for something; declaration — a statement that your answers are true; if applicable — only if it applies to you; proof of identity — documents that show who you are; certified copy — a copy an authorised person (like a pharmacist or JP) has checked against the original.

**Case study:** fake pages looked like the real sign-in form and captured details; check the web address ends in .gov.au and that you got there yourself, not from a link; don't click: type my.gov.au yourself or use the app, and report it.

realityCheck: **Privacy first.** Never collect real TFNs or ask students to share their address aloud. Made-up details are fine for practice.
**Forms are very real for some students.** Some already handle forms for their families, including for parents with limited English. Treat them as experts.
**Processes change.** TFN and Medicare application steps change often. Check the ATO and Services Australia pages before you teach, rather than relying on the details here.
**Handwriting matters.** Block letters are a skill. Give students time to practise before the final mission.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's short and practical, and pairs well with Read Your Payslip and Crack the Job Ad.
